title: The Last Inventory
premise: Freya Coldharbour, a night librarian who has spent twenty years perfecting the art of being left alone, discovers that the crumbling house where she grew up — and from which she fled at seventeen — is going to auction. The estate belongs to Marlowe Finch, the foster brother she has never forgiven for the fire that scattered their found family, and his dying wish is that she catalog the house's contents before strangers carry it away. Sorting through the inventory of her childhood, Freya uncovers letters and photographs proving the fire was not what she believed, forcing her to choose between the loyalty that kept her silent and the truth that could reunite the family she abandoned. In the end, Freya testifies at the auction hearing, saves the house as a community archive run by her old household, and forgives both Marlowe and herself.
about_author: Ines Vane is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's lives before turning to fiction about the objects we cannot put down. She writes at night, in libraries, in cities that never quite sleep.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A night shift at the Halloway Branch Library establishes her rituals: shelving, tea, deflecting a chatty patron named Odile with her practiced smile. A letter arrives addressed to 'F. Coldharbour, keeper of quiet things' — an auction notice for 14 Lantern Row. Emotional beat: loneliness revealed as armor, and the first crack in it.

chapters.title: Fourteen Lantern Row
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She walks past the boarded-up house at dawn, unable to go in, remembering only fragments: a kitchen table, six mismatched chairs, smoke. The auctioneer's sign lists the seller: M. Finch. Her hands shake on the railings. Emotional beat: dread and longing tangled together; the past is literally fenced off from her.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At home she digs out the one photograph she kept — the household on the porch, summer before the fire — and studies the boy beside her, Marlowe, whose face she has spent years refusing to remember clearly. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into resentment; she decides to attend the preview out of spite, telling herself it's closure.

chapters.title: Preview Day
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, shifting briefly to the auctioneer Tam Osei. At the preview, the house is stripped and tagged like a body. Tam mistakes her for a buyer; she corrects him — 'I lived here' — and he offers her work: catalog the contents properly before sale, paid by the estate. Emotional beat: reluctant re-entry through transaction rather than forgiveness.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Cruelties
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. First day cataloging: she inventories the kitchen, finding the sixth chair, a burn mark shaped like a hand. Flashback threads introduce the household — Mama Ruth, twins Sef and Idris, old Petal, Marlowe. Emotional beat: tenderness ambushed by memory; she works faster to outrun feeling.

chapters.title: Marlowe Comes Home
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. He arrives gaunt and ill, having sold his life abroad to buy time — literal time, weeks of it. He asks Freya not to leave before they finish the inventory. Their first conversation in twenty years is all logistics and barbed courtesy. Emotional beat: two people negotiating a truce neither trusts.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Working room by room, they collide over the hallway where the fire started. Each remembers a different version: Freya saw Marlowe running from the stairs; Marlowe says he was pulling Petal out. Neither yields. Emotional beat: the central wound reopened; loyalty to one's own memory versus another's truth.

chapters.title: Odile at the Door
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Odile appears at the house with soup and no explanation of how she found her, revealing she once lived on Lantern Row too — a neighbor child Freya never noticed. Emotional beat: found family extending beyond the original six; Freya's isolation shown as choice, not fate.

chapters.title: The Locked Room
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Upstairs, a door Marlowe refuses to open — Mama Ruth's room. He claims the key is lost. Freya picks the lock that night alone and finds Ruth's desk, locked drawers, and a wall of photographs including ones taken after Freya fled. Emotional beat: transgression and discovery; the house begins giving up its secrets.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In Ruth's desk: dozens of unsent letters — to Freya, to Marlowe, to the twins — written across twenty years. One, dated months after the fire, hints that Ruth knew the fire was set deliberately and by whom. Emotional beat: vertigo; the woman who raised them was keeping a case file on them all.

chapters.title: Sef and Idris
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. He confesses he has tracked the twins for years: Sef runs boats up the coast; Idris hasn't answered a letter since the funeral. He begs Freya to come with him to find Sef because Sef will only speak to her. Emotional beat: alliance forming out of shared guilt rather than trust.

chapters.title: The Harbor Road
chapters.summary: Dual POV, road trip chapter. They find Sef mid-haul, hard and unforgiving. He tells them the version of the fire night he saw: Marlowe carrying Petal out, and someone else leaving by the garden gate — someone small. Emotional beat: testimony that cracks Freya's certainty; the stranger in the photograph may be herself.

chapters.title: Someone Small
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, nightmarish and interior. On the drive back she reconstructs the night: she was awake, she went down for water, she smelled smoke first — and said nothing, ever, because saying something meant admitting she'd been there. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing her silence protected herself, not anyone else.

chapters.title: Petal's Box
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Back at the house, cataloging resumes; inside a hatbox labeled for Petal (now in a care home) are matches, a scorched curtain scrap, and a note in Petal's childish hand: 'I didn't mean the whole house.' Emotional beat: devastating pity replacing blame; the fire was a child's accident everyone else turned into a story.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Freya and Marlowe, dual POV. They visit Petal, elderly and lucid in flashes. She doesn't remember the fire but remembers Freya leaving without goodbye, and asks why nobody visits. Marlowe admits he paid for this home for years, anonymously. Emotional beat: love expressed as logistics; forgiveness beginning in the body before the mind allows it.

chapters.title: The Auction Looms
chapters.summary: Tam Osei's POV. Tam, sympathetic now, warns them the sale proceeds Friday; a developer plans demolition. He reveals the estate's debts mean only a formal objection — proof of historical or community significance — can delay it. Emotional beat: external clock tightening; private reckoning must become public act.

chapters.title: Idris Answers
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Using Ruth's last unsent letter's address, Freya writes to Idris; he calls at 3 a.m. He knew about Petal — Ruth told him — and stayed away because the family chose stories over each other. He'll return only if Freya tells the truth publicly, whatever it costs her. Emotional beat: the price of reunion named aloud.

chapters.title: What Freya Knew
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, confessional. She tells Marlowe everything: she was downstairs, she saw nothing but smelled everything, and her silence let him wear the suspicion for twenty years while she played the wounded one. He doesn't absolve her; he just sits with her until dawn. Emotional beat: climax of the internal arc — truth offered without guarantee of forgiveness.

chapters.title: Objection
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. At the auction hearing, Freya submits the inventory, Ruth's letters, and her own statement: the house matters because its people do. Sef arrives unannounced; Idris watches from the back. The developer's lawyer dismantles sentiment until Tam produces records of the Row's founding as a refuge home. Emotional beat: public climax; private truths weaponized for preservation.

chapters.title: The Verdict and the Sixth Chair
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The sale is stayed pending community purchase; the household scrambles — Sef's money, Marlowe's remainder, Odile's organizing, Tam's paperwork. In the emptied kitchen they set out six chairs around the table they bought back at auction. Emotional beat: exhausted, fragile victory; the shape of family reassembled from furniture and stubbornness.

chapters.title: Catalog Complete
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Marlowe, sicker now, finishes the final inventory entry himself: item one, the house; item two, its people; item three, pending. He asks Freya to keep the archive when he's gone. She says yes — the first unconditional yes she has given anyone in the book. Emotional beat: mortality met with steadiness instead of flight.

chapters.title: Lantern Row, After
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, epilogue a year later. The house is the Lantern Row Community Archive; Odile runs Saturday openings; Petal visits in good weather. Freya still works nights at the library but her smile now starts conversations. Final image: she hangs the porch photograph, all six of them, above the catalog desk. Emotional beat: resolution — identity rebuilt not despite the past but as its honest custodian.
